justice: The wide concrete road provides shared space for multiple users, but there is no clearly designated sidewalk, so pedestrian space is not equitably separated from vehicle space.
No visible curb ramps, tactile paving, marked crossings, or other barrier-free elements are present, limiting accessibility for users with different mobility needs.
The unpaved edges, loose stones, and construction-like debris near the roadside create uneven conditions that distribute usable space unfairly toward able-bodied users.
The road appears passable for cars and pedestrians, but the lack of lane markings or formal user hierarchy means vulnerable users receive limited protected space.
safety: There is no visible sidewalk or protected pedestrian path, so people walking on the concrete roadway may mix directly with trucks and cars.
A truck is parked or moving close to the road edge on the right, indicating potential conflict between large vehicles and pedestrians in a narrow shared carriageway.
The road curves around the central tree island, which may reduce sightlines between approaching vehicles and pedestrians.
Overhead transmission infrastructure and a utility corridor dominate the setting, while no visible street lighting or traffic calming devices are present.
livability: The area appears low-density and quiet, but there are few visible amenities such as shops, seating, bus stops, or community facilities that support daily street life.
Three pedestrians are present, showing some local use, yet the street lacks social infrastructure like benches, active frontages, or gathering spaces.
The houses are set back behind open yards and rough edges, which reduces enclosure and makes the street feel more utilitarian than vibrant.
Some trees and open ground provide a semi-rural character, but the nearby truck and industrial-looking utility structures weaken residential livability.
sustainability: Several mature trees along the center and right side provide some greenery and limited ecological value.
The street shows no visible bike lane, bus stop, or public transport feature that would support low-carbon travel choices.
Large paved and bare-soil surfaces dominate, with no obvious rain gardens, permeable landscaping strategy, or stormwater management elements.
The prominent high-voltage transmission tower and vehicle-oriented road environment suggest an infrastructure-heavy setting with limited human-scaled green design.
aesthetics: The row of low traditional-style houses gives the street some local character and visual identity.
However, exposed dirt, rubble piles, rough road edges, and scattered materials reduce visual neatness and overall streetscape quality.
The large transmission tower and overhead power lines strongly dominate the skyline, creating a harsh industrial visual presence.
Trees soften parts of the scene, but the overall composition remains plain and somewhat neglected rather than visually refined.
comfort: Trees near the center-right provide some shade, but most of the road remains exposed, so thermal comfort is only moderate.
The main concrete roadway looks relatively smooth for walking and driving, but the unpaved edges and loose stones reduce physical comfort off the main path.
There are no visible benches, shelters, or resting places, limiting comfort for users who may need to stop or wait outdoors.
The area appears low traffic and not crowded, which likely improves acoustic and psychological comfort compared with busier streets.
walkability: People are walking directly on the road, indicating that pedestrian movement is possible, but the absence of sidewalks greatly weakens walkability.
The concrete surface is fairly continuous and wide, supporting basic movement, yet the curved alignment and lack of crossings reduce pedestrian clarity.
Roadside dirt shoulders, rubble, and uneven edges create poor walking margins and weaken route quality.
Trees add limited shade and visual relief, but there are no pedestrian signs, crossings, or frontage activities to make walking especially attractive.
bikeability: No bike lane, shoulder marking, or separated cycling facility is visible anywhere on the road.
Cyclists would need to share space directly with trucks and cars on a curving roadway, which reduces perceived and actual cycling safety.
The concrete surface may be rideable in the center, but rough edges, dirt shoulders, and roadside debris make recovery space poor for bicycles.
No bicycle parking, signage, or intersection treatments are present to support cycling convenience or legitimacy.
